source: Alexander, P. 2010. 'Large Ruminant Reproduction Workshop', ACIAR AH 2005/086, presented in Cambodia (mekonglivestock.wordpress.com). Only the practically farmer-relevant sections are extracted here; the source also covers advanced reproductive technologies (AI, embryo transfer, cloning) that are academic/veterinary-training content rather than farmer-facing and were excluded from this batch.
text: Nutrition is described as the single most important factor affecting reproductive performance in cattle, explaining much of the regional variation seen even within one country -- it affects both the calving-to-first-heat interval and conception rate. Body condition score (BCS) of the mother at calving is highlighted as the most important individual factor: a BCS of 3-4 at calving supports a quicker return to heat, readiness for the next mating, and enough milk to properly raise the calf. Tropical pasture and crop by-products commonly fed to cattle often have crude protein content below 7.5%, which reduces rumen efficiency and digestibility and can cause cows to lose weight after calving. Underfeeding has its largest impact on lactating cows and young stock, showing up as reduced milk yield, reduced calf growth, reduced weaning rates, delayed puberty in replacement heifers, and reduced lifetime reproductive potential -- the source cites research finding heifers on a restricted diet reaching puberty months later than well-fed heifers, and reaching puberty at a consistent body weight regardless of age, underscoring that it's the animal's condition, not just its age, that determines reproductive readiness.
